concepts.name: Constitutional Position of Governor: Nature and Dual Role
key_dimensions: Governor as constitutional head vs. agent of Centre — Article 153–167 framework
Sarkaria Commission vs. Punchhi Commission views on Governor's dual character
Comparison with President: similarities and critical differences (e.g., no Council of State, no impeachment equivalent)
Supreme Court in S.R. Bommai (1994) on Governor's role and limitations

concepts.name: Appointment of Governor: Procedure, Conventions and Controversies
key_dimensions: Article 155 & 156 — appointment by President (warrant under hand and seal), pleasure doctrine
Constitutional silence on consultation with Chief Minister — convention vs. practice (Sarkaria Commission recommendation of mandatory consultation)
Eligibility conditions under Article 157 — citizen, 35 years, not holding office of profit; trap: no residency requirement for the state
Controversy over appointing sitting politicians/retired bureaucrats — Punchhi Commission reforms vs. current practice

concepts.name: Term of Office, Removal and Holdover Doctrine
key_dimensions: Article 156 — 5-year term 'at the pleasure of the President'; no fixed tenure guarantee
Holdover doctrine: Governor continues until successor takes charge — trap: not a right, merely a convention
B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010): SC ruling that pleasure doctrine cannot be exercised arbitrarily; reasons must exist though need not be disclosed
Comparison: Governor cannot be removed by State Legislature or impeached — contrast with President

concepts.name: Qualifications, Conditions of Office and Oath
key_dimensions: Article 157 (qualifications) vs. Article 158 (conditions) — UPSC frequently tests overlap
Article 158 prohibitions: cannot be Member of Parliament or State Legislature, cannot hold office of profit
Oath administered by Chief Justice of High Court (or senior-most judge) — trap: NOT by President or Speaker
Emoluments charged to Consolidated Fund of State — cannot be reduced during term (Article 158(4))

concepts.name: Discretionary Powers of Governor: Constitutional vs. Situational Discretion
key_dimensions: Article 163 — Council of Ministers to aid and advise except where Governor acts in 'discretion' — no exhaustive list in Constitution
Constitutional discretion (explicit): Reservation of bills, report to President under Article 356, assent to bills when Legislature is not in session
Situational/conventional discretion: Appointment of CM when no clear majority, dismissal of government losing majority
Trap: Governor has far more discretion than President — President has almost no personal discretion after 44th Amendment

concepts.name: Appointment of Chief Minister and Council of Ministers by Governor
key_dimensions: Article 164 — CM appointed by Governor; other ministers on CM's advice; collective responsibility to Legislative Assembly
Hung Assembly scenarios: Governor's discretion in inviting the leader — Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006) on floor test
Goa, Manipur, Bihar controversies — post-election horse-trading and Governor's role in government formation
Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker (2016) — SC on limits of Governor's power to summon/prorogue assembly to prevent floor test

concepts.name: Governor's Legislative Powers: Summoning, Proroguing and Dissolving the Assembly
key_dimensions: Article 174 — Governor summons, prorogues sessions; Article 174(2)(b) — dissolution of Legislative Assembly
Dissolution only on CM's advice in normal circumstances — trap: Governor cannot dissolve suo motu except in specific circumstances
Nabam Rebia case: SC held Governor cannot advance session or remove Speaker to prevent floor test — limits on Article 174
Difference between prorogation (terminates session, bills lapse in some cases) vs. dissolution (terminates House, all pending business lapses)

concepts.name: Governor's Role in Assent to State Bills: Four Options and Withholding Assent
key_dimensions: Article 200 — four options: give assent, withhold assent, return bill (except Money Bill) for reconsideration, reserve for President's consideration
Trap: If Legislature passes bill again after return, Governor MUST give assent — no second veto (unlike reservation for President)
Reservation for President: mandatory in certain cases (Article 200 proviso) — e.g., bills derogating High Court powers
Recent controversies: Kerala, Punjab, Telangana Governors sitting on bills indefinitely — SC in State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor (2023) on 'pocket veto'

concepts.name: Governor's Ordinance Making Power: Scope, Limitations and Misuse
key_dimensions: Article 213 — Governor can promulgate ordinances when Legislature not in session; requires President's instructions in some cases
Limitations: Cannot override fundamental rights, cannot legislate on matters requiring President's assent, cannot be repromulgated indefinitely (D.C. Wadhwa case 1987)
D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar: SC struck down ordinance raj — repromulgation subverts democratic process; ordinances are temporary measures
Trap: Governor cannot promulgate ordinance on subjects in State List without President's prior instructions if similar bill was rejected by Legislature

concepts.name: Governor's Report under Article 356 and Role in President's Rule
key_dimensions: Article 356 — President's Rule imposed on Governor's report OR otherwise (President can act without Governor's report)
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994): Floor test mandatory before recommending President's Rule; report must be based on objective material
Governor's report is not justiciable per se, but imposition of President's Rule is subject to judicial review — Bommai
Trap: Governor's report is advisory, not binding on President; President can impose rule 'otherwise' too — misuse potential

concepts.name: Governor as Chancellor of State Universities: Extra-Constitutional Role
key_dimensions: Governor as ex-officio Chancellor under state university acts — not a constitutional provision but statutory
Recent conflicts: Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal — state governments attempting to remove Governor as Chancellor via state legislation
Limits: State can legislate on universities (State List Entry 32) — can it divest Governor of Chancellorship? Constitutional questions
Conflict between Governor (Centre's agent) and elected government over university appointments (Vice-Chancellors) — judicial interventions

concepts.name: Governor's Special Responsibilities and Directions under Sixth Schedule
key_dimensions: Sixth Schedule areas (tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram) — Governor has special discretionary powers regarding Autonomous District Councils
Article 371 series — special provisions for certain states (Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal) — Governor's special responsibility
Trap: In states under Article 371(A) (Nagaland), Governor has special responsibility regarding law and order — acts in personal judgment, not on CM's advice
Distinction between special responsibility (Governor acts independently) vs. normal functioning (acts on CM's advice)

concepts.name: Immunity and Privileges of Governor: Article 361
key_dimensions: Article 361 — Governor not answerable to any court for exercise of powers and duties; cannot be arrested or imprisoned during term
Civil proceedings require 2 months' notice; criminal proceedings cannot be initiated during term
Trap: Immunity is for official acts — personal acts may not be covered; also immunity does not mean unaccountability (SC can review constitutionality)
Rameshwar Prasad case: SC examined Governor's action despite Article 361 — action can be challenged even if Governor personally immune

concepts.name: Governor's Financial Powers: Role in Budget and Money Bills
key_dimensions: Annual Financial Statement (budget) laid before Legislature on Governor's recommendation — Article 202
Money Bills can only be introduced in Legislative Assembly on Governor's recommendation — Article 207; trap: no recommendation = bill cannot be introduced
Demand for grants requires Governor's recommendation; Legislature cannot increase grants
Governor's assent to Appropriation Bill and Finance Bill — cannot withhold assent (conventions vs. discretion debate)

concepts.name: Governor's Judicial Powers: Pardon, Reprieve and Appointment of HC Judges
key_dimensions: Article 161 — pardoning power for offences against state laws; excludes court-martial offences (unlike President under Article 72)
Critical trap: Governor CANNOT pardon death sentence — only President can under Article 72; Governor can only suspend, remit or commute death sentence
Role in appointment of High Court judges: Article 217 — consultation with Governor (along with President, CJI, Chief Justice of HC) — Governor's role is consultative
Governor appoints Advocate General (Article 165) — on CM's advice; not a discretionary power

concepts.name: Relationship Between Governor and State Cabinet: Article 163 and Binding Nature of Advice
key_dimensions: Article 163(1) — Council of Ministers to aid and advise Governor; Article 163(3) — Governor's decision on discretion is final and cannot be questioned in court
44th Amendment analogy: Unlike President (bound by cabinet advice after 1978), Governor's binding by cabinet advice is not constitutionally explicit — area of controversy
Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab (1974): SC held Governor generally acts on cabinet advice; discretion is exception, not rule
Trap: Governor can return cabinet advice once for reconsideration but must act on re-tendered advice — no explicit constitutional provision, but convention

concepts.name: Comparison: Governor vs. Lieutenant Governor (Union Territories)
key_dimensions: Governor (Article 153) represents President in states; LG (Article 239) directly administers on behalf of President in UTs
LG of Delhi — Article 239AA special status; elected government vs. LG conflict — Government of NCT of Delhi v. Union of India (2018 and 2023 Constitution Bench)
Trap: LG of Puducherry has similar tension with elected CM — LG's powers wider in UT than Governor's in state
Governor has no role in Union List matters in state; LG in UT can act on Union List without elected government's advice

concepts.name: Post-Election Scenarios: Governor's Discretion in Government Formation — Key Case Laws
key_dimensions: Sequence of invitation: Single largest party vs. pre-poll alliance vs. post-poll alliance — Sarkaria Commission guidelines
Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India (2006): Governor cannot impose President's Rule merely to benefit a particular party; must explore all possibilities
Goa 2017, Karnataka 2018: SC intervened to direct immediate floor tests — limiting Governor's discretion in delaying floor test
Trap: Governor CANNOT ask a party to prove majority in the Governor's house — floor test must happen in Legislative Assembly only

concepts.name: Reservation of State Bills for President's Consideration: Scope and Presidential Options
key_dimensions: Article 200 proviso + Article 201 — when bill is reserved, President may give assent, withhold assent, or (if not Money Bill) direct return for reconsideration
Trap: If Legislature passes bill again after President returns it, President is NOT bound to give assent (unlike Governor's situation) — President can sit on it
Mandatory reservation cases: Bills derogating HC powers (Article 200), bills in State List that conflict with Parliamentary legislation, bills during National Emergency
Recent controversy: Governor reserving bills without time limit — SC in 2023 ruling (Kerala/Punjab cases) that Governor cannot indefinitely delay — must act within reasonable time

concepts.name: Recommendations of Sarkaria and Punchhi Commissions on Governorship
key_dimensions: Sarkaria Commission (1988): Governor should be eminent person, not active politician; consult CM before appointment; should not be from ruling party at Centre
Punchhi Commission (2010): Fixed 5-year term should be protected; removal only through impeachment-like process; inter-state council to be consulted
Trap: Neither commission's recommendations are legally binding — they are advisory; constitutional provisions remain unchanged
UPSC angle: Compare recommendations with current practice — where divergence exists is a high-yield exam area (e.g., appointment of active politicians, mid-term transfers)
